claim: CERS1 abundance declines with aging in human skeletal muscle cells.
source: In humans, CERS1 abundance declines with aging in skeletal muscle cells and, correlates with biological pathways involved in muscle function and myogenesis.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing reduced CERS1 transcript levels in aged compared to young myoblasts (Figure 1B).

claim: CERS1 correlates with biological pathways involved in muscle function and myogenesis in humans.
source: In humans, CERS1 abundance declines with aging in skeletal muscle cells and, correlates with biological pathways involved in muscle function and myogenesis.
evidence: Supported by gene set enrichment analysis showing CERS1 correlating transcripts are enriched in muscle contraction and myogenesis pathways (Figure 1C).

claim: CERS1 is upregulated during myogenic differentiation.
source: Furthermore, CERS1 is upregulated during myogenic differentiation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing upregulation of Cers1/CERS1 at several timepoints once muscle differentiation was induced in mouse and human muscle cells (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of CERS1 in aged mice blunts myogenesis.
source: Pharmacological or genetic inhibition of CERS1 in aged mice blunts myogenesis and deteriorates aged skeletal muscle mass and function, which is associated with the occurrence of morphological features typical of inflammation and fibrosis.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing P053 treatment downregulated expression of myogenic regulatory factors and myosin heavy chain transcripts in aged mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of CERS1 in aged mice deteriorates aged skeletal muscle mass and function.
source: Pharmacological or genetic inhibition of CERS1 in aged mice blunts myogenesis and deteriorates aged skeletal muscle mass and function, which is associated with the occurrence of morphological features typical of inflammation and fibrosis.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing P053 administration reduced lean body mass (Figure 2H), grip strength (Figure 2I), and treadmill running performance (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F–G) in aged mice.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of CERS1 in aged mice is associated with the occurrence of morphological features typical of inflammation and fibrosis.
source: Pharmacological or genetic inhibition of CERS1 in aged mice blunts myogenesis and deteriorates aged skeletal muscle mass and function, which is associated with the occurrence of morphological features typical of inflammation and fibrosis.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing P053 treatment led to increased fibrosis (Figure 2F), occurrence of centralized nuclei (Figure 2G), and increased CD45+ cells (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).

claim: Genetic inhibition of CERS1 in aged mice blunts myogenesis.
source: Pharmacological or genetic inhibition of CERS1 in aged mice blunts myogenesis and deteriorates aged skeletal muscle mass and function, which is associated with the occurrence of morphological features typical of inflammation and fibrosis.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing AAV9-mediated silencing of Cers1 downregulated expression of myogenic regulatory factors and myosin heavy chains (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).

claim: Genetic inhibition of CERS1 in aged mice deteriorates aged skeletal muscle mass and function.
source: Pharmacological or genetic inhibition of CERS1 in aged mice blunts myogenesis and deteriorates aged skeletal muscle mass and function, which is associated with the occurrence of morphological features typical of inflammation and fibrosis.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing AAV9-mediated silencing of Cers1 reduced muscle mass (Figure 3H), grip strength (Figure 3I), and running performance (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–C) in aged mice.

claim: Ablation of the CERS1 orthologue lagr-1 in Caenorhabditis elegans exacerbates the age-associated decline in muscle function and integrity.
source: Ablation of the CERS1 orthologue lagr-1 in Caenorhabditis elegans similarly exacerbates the age-associated decline in muscle function and integrity.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing lagr-1 RNAi reduced worm muscle function (Figure 4F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D) and deteriorated muscle fiber morphology (Figure 4G).

claim: Genetic variants reduce CERS1 expression in human skeletal muscle.
source: We discover genetic variants reducing CERS1 expression in human skeletal muscle and Mendelian randomization analysis in the UK biobank cohort shows that these variants reduce muscle grip strength and overall health.
evidence: Supported by data from the GTEx dataset showing three independent genetic variants (rs117558072, rs1122821, rs71332140) significantly alter CERS1 expression in human skeletal muscle (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).

claim: Genetic variants reducing CERS1 expression reduce muscle grip strength in humans.
source: We discover genetic variants reducing CERS1 expression in human skeletal muscle and Mendelian randomization analysis in the UK biobank cohort shows that these variants reduce muscle grip strength and overall health.
evidence: Supported by Mendelian randomization analysis in the UK biobank showing CERS1 expression reducing alleles decrease right and left grip strength (Figure 5A, Figure 5B).

claim: Genetic variants reducing CERS1 expression reduce overall health in humans.
source: We discover genetic variants reducing CERS1 expression in human skeletal muscle and Mendelian randomization analysis in the UK biobank cohort shows that these variants reduce muscle grip strength and overall health.
evidence: Supported by Mendelian randomization analysis in the UK biobank showing CERS1 expression reducing alleles decrease overall health rating (Figure 5A, Figure 5B).

claim: CERS1 transcript levels are reduced in aged compared to young human myoblasts.
source: We found reduced CERS1 transcript levels in aged compared to young myoblasts which is in line with the previous report in whole muscle tissue (Tosetti et al., 2020; Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurement of CERS1 expression in primary muscle cells isolated from young and old human donors (Figure 1B).

claim: Cers1 expression in skeletal muscle tissue correlates negatively with aging.
source: Among these, Cers1 expression in skeletal muscle tissue was shown to correlate negatively with aging (Tosetti et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Molecular pathways involved in muscle contraction and myogenesis are among the strongest correlating pathways with CERS1 in human skeletal muscle.
source: Molecular pathways involved in muscle contraction and myogenesis were among the strongest correlating pathways (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by gene set enrichment analysis of CERS1 correlating transcripts in human skeletal muscle biopsies (Figure 1C).

claim: CERS1 expression correlates positively with transcripts involved in myogenesis (MYF5, MYH2, MYH7, MYL1).
source: In line with this finding, we also observed significant positive correlations of CERS1 expression with transcripts involved in myogenesis (MYF5, MYH2, MYH7, MYL1; Figure 1D) and muscle contraction (TPM2, ACTA1, TMOD2, TNN1; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis in the GTEx dataset (Figure 1D).

claim: CERS1 expression correlates positively with transcripts involved in muscle contraction (TPM2, ACTA1, TMOD2, TNN1).
source: In line with this finding, we also observed significant positive correlations of CERS1 expression with transcripts involved in myogenesis (MYF5, MYH2, MYH7, MYL1; Figure 1D) and muscle contraction (TPM2, ACTA1, TMOD2, TNN1; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis in the GTEx dataset (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).

claim: C18:1 ceramide increases during mouse myoblast maturation.
source: Measurement of ceramide levels during myogenic differentiation confirmed particularly the increase of C18:1 during mouse myoblast maturation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), whereas C14:0, C22:0, as well as C18:0 ceramide species were found to be induced during human myoblast differentiation suggesting some species-specific effects (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by measurement of ceramide levels during myogenic differentiation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).

claim: C14:0, C22:0, and C18:0 ceramide species are induced during human myoblast differentiation.
source: Measurement of ceramide levels during myogenic differentiation confirmed particularly the increase of C18:1 during mouse myoblast maturation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), whereas C14:0, C22:0, as well as C18:0 ceramide species were found to be induced during human myoblast differentiation suggesting some species-specific effects (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by measurement of ceramide levels during myogenic differentiation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).

claim: P053 inhibits mouse skeletal muscle cell differentiation.
source: Importantly, the CERS1-specific pharmacological inhibitor P053, which has been shown to reduce fat mass (Turner et al., 2018), inhibited mouse and human skeletal muscle cell differentiation as evidenced by downregulated expression of the early expressed myogenic transcription factors Myog/MYOG and Myf6/MYF6 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E and Figure 1F) as well as of myosin light- and heavy chains (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F–G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing downregulated expression of myogenic transcription factors and myosin chains in P053-treated cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F–G).

claim: P053 inhibits human skeletal muscle cell differentiation.
source: Importantly, the CERS1-specific pharmacological inhibitor P053, which has been shown to reduce fat mass (Turner et al., 2018), inhibited mouse and human skeletal muscle cell differentiation as evidenced by downregulated expression of the early expressed myogenic transcription factors Myog/MYOG and Myf6/MYF6 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E and Figure 1F) as well as of myosin light- and heavy chains (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F–G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing downregulated expression of myogenic transcription factors and myosin chains in P053-treated cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F–G).

claim: P053 has been shown to reduce fat mass.
source: Importantly, the CERS1-specific pharmacological inhibitor P053, which has been shown to reduce fat mass (Turner et al., 2018), inhibited mouse and human skeletal muscle cell differentiation as evidenced by downregulated expression of the early expressed myogenic transcription factors Myog/MYOG and Myf6/MYF6 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E and Figure 1F) as well as of myosin light- and heavy chains (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F–G).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Turner et al., 2018).

claim: Systemic administration of P053 over 6 months reduced C18:0 and C18:1 ceramides in skeletal muscle tissue.
source: As expected, systemic administration of P053 over 6 months (Figure 2A) reduced C18:0 and C18:1 ceramides in skeletal muscle tissue (Figure 2B), suggesting that P053 indeed targeted Cers1 as previously shown (Turner et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by measurement of ceramide levels in skeletal muscle tissue of P053-treated mice (Figure 2B).

claim: P053 treatment increased C24:0/C24:1 ceramides in skeletal muscle tissue.
source: Interestingly, this was coupled with an increase in C24:0 /C24:1 ceramides (Figure 2B) and C24:0 /C24:1 dihydroceramides (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), which are synthesized by Cers2 (Mizutani et al., 2005; Ben-David et al., 2011; Laviad et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by measurement of ceramide levels in skeletal muscle tissue of P053-treated mice (Figure 2B).

claim: P053 treatment increased C24:0/C24:1 dihydroceramides in skeletal muscle tissue.
source: Interestingly, this was coupled with an increase in C24:0 /C24:1 ceramides (Figure 2B) and C24:0 /C24:1 dihydroceramides (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), which are synthesized by Cers2 (Mizutani et al., 2005; Ben-David et al., 2011; Laviad et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by measurement of dihydroceramide levels in skeletal muscle tissue of P053-treated mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).

claim: C24:0/C24:1 ceramides are synthesized by Cers2.
source: Interestingly, this was coupled with an increase in C24:0 /C24:1 ceramides (Figure 2B) and C24:0 /C24:1 dihydroceramides (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), which are synthesized by Cers2 (Mizutani et al., 2005; Ben-David et al., 2011; Laviad et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Mizutani et al., 2005; Ben-David et al., 2011; Laviad et al., 2008).

claim: An increase in C24:0/C24:1 ceramide and dihydroceramides upon Cers1 inhibition is in line with previous reports on Cers1 inhibition.
source: An increase in C24:0 /C24:1 ceramide and dihydroceramides upon Cers1 inhibition is in line with a previous reports on Cers1 inhibition (Turner et al., 2018; Tosetti et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Turner et al., 2018; Tosetti et al., 2020).

claim: Fiber size is reduced upon aging in mice.
source: Laminin staining (Figure 2C) followed by minimum ferret diameter measurement (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) and fiber size distribution (Figure 2D) showed that fiber size was reduced upon aging with a frequency shift towards smaller muscle fibers.
evidence: Supported by laminin staining and fiber size measurements (Figure 2C, Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).

claim: P053 treatment exacerbates the age-related reduction in muscle fiber size.
source: Laminin staining (Figure 2C) followed by minimum ferret diameter measurement (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) and fiber size distribution (Figure 2D) showed that fiber size was reduced upon aging with a frequency shift towards smaller muscle fibers. Treatment with P053 exacerbated this age-related reduction in muscle fiber size.
evidence: Supported by laminin staining and fiber size measurements showing further reduction with P053 treatment (Figure 2C, Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).

claim: The trained cellpose model achieved an Average Precision of 0.97±0.02 for detecting skeletal muscle fibers.
source: Using our trained model in muscle sections stained with laminin and CD45, we were able to capture most muscle fibers (Average Precision: 0.97±0.02, n=4, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by validation metrics of the trained cellpose model.

claim: There is an age-related decrease in muscle cross-sectional area in mice.
source: Results showed an age-related decrease in cross-sectional area, which worsened with P053 treatment (Figure 2E, top and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) and is in agreement with our manual curation of fiber diameter (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: Supported by automated detection of muscle fibers showing decreased cross-sectional area with age (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).

claim: P053 treatment worsens the age-related decrease in muscle cross-sectional area.
source: Results showed an age-related decrease in cross-sectional area, which worsened with P053 treatment (Figure 2E, top and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) and is in agreement with our manual curation of fiber diameter (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: Supported by automated detection of muscle fibers showing further decreased cross-sectional area with P053 treatment (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).

claim: There is an increase in CD45+ cells neighboring muscle fibers with age and P053 treatment.
source: We also observed an increase in CD45+ neighboring muscle fibers with age and P053 treatment (Figure 2E, bottom).
evidence: Supported by automated detection of CD45+ signal intensities adjacent to muscle fibers (Figure 2E).

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of Cers1 led to increased fibrosis in aged mice.
source: Analyses of other morphological markers of skeletal muscle aging, fibrosis and centralized nuclei, revealed that pharmacological inhibition of Cers1 led to increased fibrosis (Figure 2F) and occurrence of centralized nuclei (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by Sirius red staining showing increased fibrosis in P053-treated aged mice (Figure 2F).

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of Cers1 led to increased occurrence of centralized nuclei in aged mice.
source: Analyses of other morphological markers of skeletal muscle aging, fibrosis and centralized nuclei, revealed that pharmacological inhibition of Cers1 led to increased fibrosis (Figure 2F) and occurrence of centralized nuclei (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by hematoxylin/eosin staining showing increased centralized nuclei in P053-treated aged mice (Figure 2G).

claim: Lean body mass is reduced upon aging in mice.
source: Lean body mass was reduced upon aging and aged mice treated with P053 presented further reductions in muscle mass (Figure 2H), which is in line with reduced fiber diameters (Figure 2C–D) and cross-section area (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by phenotyping measurements showing reduced lean body mass in aged mice (Figure 2H).

claim: Aged mice treated with P053 presented further reductions in muscle mass.
source: Lean body mass was reduced upon aging and aged mice treated with P053 presented further reductions in muscle mass (Figure 2H), which is in line with reduced fiber diameters (Figure 2C–D) and cross-section area (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by phenotyping measurements showing further reduced lean body mass in P053-treated aged mice (Figure 2H).

claim: P053 administration worsened the effect of aging by reducing grip strength in aged mice.
source: Measurement of functional muscle parameters revealed that P053 administration worsened the effect of aging by reducing grip strength (Figure 2I) and treadmill running performance in aged mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F–G).
evidence: Supported by grip strength measurements showing reduced grip strength in P053-treated aged mice (Figure 2I).

claim: P053 administration worsened the effect of aging by reducing treadmill running performance in aged mice.
source: Measurement of functional muscle parameters revealed that P053 administration worsened the effect of aging by reducing grip strength (Figure 2I) and treadmill running performance in aged mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F–G).
evidence: Supported by treadmill running measurements showing reduced running time and distance in P053-treated aged mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F–G).

claim: Genetic knockout of Cers1 in young mice impaired muscle contractility.
source: Our observation of pharmacologic Cers1 inhibition in aged mice is in line with a previous study where genetic knockout of Cers1 in young mice impaired muscle contractility (Tosetti et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Tosetti et al., 2020).

claim: A single intramuscular injection of AAV9 with shRNA against mouse Cers1 in 18-month-old mice reduced Cers1 mRNA expression by approximately 50% at 24 months of age.
source: A single intramuscular injection of AAV9 with short hairpin RNA (shRNA) against mouse Cers1 (Figure 3A) in 18-month-old mice reduced Cers1 mRNA expression by ≈ 50% at 24 months of age (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H) and hence, reduced C18:0 and C18:1 ceramide metabolites (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by measurement of Cers1 RNA expression in AAV9-injected mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H).

claim: AAV9-mediated genetic inhibition of Cers1 reduced C18:0 and C18:1 ceramide metabolites in aged skeletal muscle.
source: A single intramuscular injection of AAV9 with short hairpin RNA (shRNA) against mouse Cers1 (Figure 3A) in 18-month-old mice reduced Cers1 mRNA expression by ≈ 50% at 24 months of age (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H) and hence, reduced C18:0 and C18:1 ceramide metabolites (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by measurement of ceramide levels in AAV9-injected mice (Figure 3B).

claim: Genetic inhibition of Cers1 in aged skeletal muscle tended to increase Cers2-derived very long chain ceramides.
source: Similarly to our observation in P053-treated animals, genetic inhibition of Cers1 in aged skeletal muscle tended to increase Cers2-derived very long chain ceramides (Figure 3B) and dihydroceramides (Figure 2—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: Supported by measurement of ceramide levels in AAV9-injected mice (Figure 3B).

claim: Genetic inhibition of Cers1 in aged skeletal muscle tended to increase Cers2-derived very long chain dihydroceramides.
source: Similarly to our observation in P053-treated animals, genetic inhibition of Cers1 in aged skeletal muscle tended to increase Cers2-derived very long chain ceramides (Figure 3B) and dihydroceramides (Figure 2—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: Supported by measurement of dihydroceramide levels in AAV9-injected mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1I).

claim: Genetic silencing of Cers1 reduced average skeletal muscle fiber size in aged mice.
source: Genetic silencing of Cers1 reduced average skeletal muscle fiber size (Figure 3C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1J), shifting muscle fibers towards smaller fibers (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by laminin staining and fiber size measurements in AAV9-injected mice (Figure 3C, Figure 3D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1J).

claim: Cers1-deficient aged muscles had smaller cross-sectional area.
source: This was in line with our custom cellpose model for fiber detection in muscle cross-sections showing that Cers1-deficient, aged muscles had smaller cross-sectional area (Figure 3E, top and Figure 2—figure supplement 1K), and showed more signs of inflammation (Figure 3E, bottom and Figure 2—figure supplement 1L).
evidence: Supported by automated detection of muscle fibers in AAV9-injected mice (Figure 3E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1K).

claim: Cers1-deficient aged muscles showed more signs of inflammation.
source: This was in line with our custom cellpose model for fiber detection in muscle cross-sections showing that Cers1-deficient, aged muscles had smaller cross-sectional area (Figure 3E, top and Figure 2—figure supplement 1K), and showed more signs of inflammation (Figure 3E, bottom and Figure 2—figure supplement 1L).
evidence: Supported by automated detection of CD45+ signal in AAV9-injected mice (Figure 3E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1L).

claim: Ablation of Cers1 in aged muscle showed a trend towards increased fibrosis.
source: Furthermore, ablation of Cers1 in aged muscle showed a trend towards increased fibrosis (Figure 3F) and more centralized nuclei (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by Sirius red staining in AAV9-injected mice (Figure 3F).

claim: Ablation of Cers1 in aged muscle showed more centralized nuclei.
source: Furthermore, ablation of Cers1 in aged muscle showed a trend towards increased fibrosis (Figure 3F) and more centralized nuclei (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by hematoxylin/eosin staining in AAV9-injected mice (Figure 3G).

claim: Genetic targeting of Cers1 reduced muscle mass in aged mice.
source: These findings were coupled with reduced muscle mass (Figure 3H), as well as reduced muscle grip strength (Figure 3I) and running performance in Cers1-deficient aged mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: Supported by measurement of gastrocnemius muscle weight in AAV9-injected mice (Figure 3H).

claim: Genetic targeting of Cers1 reduced muscle grip strength in aged mice.
source: These findings were coupled with reduced muscle mass (Figure 3H), as well as reduced muscle grip strength (Figure 3I) and running performance in Cers1-deficient aged mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: Supported by grip strength measurements in AAV9-injected mice (Figure 3I).

claim: Genetic targeting of Cers1 reduced running performance in aged mice.
source: These findings were coupled with reduced muscle mass (Figure 3H), as well as reduced muscle grip strength (Figure 3I) and running performance in Cers1-deficient aged mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: Supported by treadmill running measurements in AAV9-injected mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–C).

claim: Reduced grip strength upon Cers1 inhibition in aged mice is in line with reduced ex vivo contraction capacity of young muscles deficient of Cers1.
source: Reduced grip strength upon Cers1 inhibition in aged mice is in line with reduced ex vivo contraction capacity of young muscles deficient of Cers1 (Tosetti et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Tosetti et al., 2020).

claim: Lentivirus-mediated silencing of Cers1 in mouse C2C12 muscle progenitor cells reduced Cers1 expression.
source: Lentivirus-mediated silencing of Cers1 using shRNA in mouse C2C12 muscle progenitor cells reduced Cers1 expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D) and with it, C18:0 /C18:1 ceramide species (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by measurement of Cers1 gene expression in lentivirus-transduced C2C12 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).

claim: Lentivirus-mediated silencing of Cers1 in mouse C2C12 muscle progenitor cells reduced C18:0/C18:1 ceramide species.
source: Lentivirus-mediated silencing of Cers1 using shRNA in mouse C2C12 muscle progenitor cells reduced Cers1 expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D) and with it, C18:0 /C18:1 ceramide species (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by measurement of ceramide levels in lentivirus-transduced C2C12 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).

claim: Lentivirus-mediated silencing of Cers1 in mouse C2C12 muscle progenitor cells increased very long chain ceramides.
source: This was coupled by an increase in potentially toxic very long chain ceramides (Figure 3E) and dihydroceramides (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by measurement of ceramide levels in lentivirus-transduced C2C12 cells (Figure 3E).

claim: Lentivirus-mediated silencing of Cers1 in mouse C2C12 muscle progenitor cells increased very long chain dihydroceramides.
source: This was coupled by an increase in potentially toxic very long chain ceramides (Figure 3E) and dihydroceramides (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by measurement of dihydroceramide levels in lentivirus-transduced C2C12 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).

claim: Differentiation of Cers1-deficient myoblasts revealed diminished myogenesis evidenced by reduced myotube diameter, myotube area and number of multinucleated myotubes.
source: Differentiation of these Cers1-deficient myoblasts towards myotubes revealed diminished myogenesis evidenced by immunostaining (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G), which shows reduced myotube diameter, myotube area and number of multinucleated myotubes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and quantification of myotube parameters in Cers1-deficient C2C12 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G, Figure 3—figure supplement 1H).

claim: Expression profiling revealed reduced transcript expression of myogenic differentiation markers in Cers1-deficient C2C12 cells.
source: Expression profiling revealed reduced transcript expression of myogenic differentiation markers (Figure 3—figure supplement 1I), further suggesting that Cers1 is indispensable for proper myogenic differentiation of mouse muscle cells.
evidence: Supported by gene expression profiling in Cers1-deficient C2C12 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1I).

claim: Cers1 inhibition did not affect protein synthesis in differentiating myoblasts.
source: Notably, Cers1 inhibition did not affect protein synthesis but upregulated the Myostatin pathway including the Foxo3/Smad3 transcription factors and its downstream E3 ubiquitin ligases, suggesting an increase in protein degradation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: Supported by Click-iT HPG assay and gene expression profiling in Cers1-deficient C2C12 cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C).

claim: Cers1 inhibition upregulated the Myostatin pathway including the Foxo3/Smad3 transcription factors and its downstream E3 ubiquitin ligases.
source: Notably, Cers1 inhibition did not affect protein synthesis but upregulated the Myostatin pathway including the Foxo3/Smad3 transcription factors and its downstream E3 ubiquitin ligases, suggesting an increase in protein degradation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: Supported by gene expression profiling in Cers1-deficient C2C12 cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).

claim: Reducing CERS1 expression in human primary myoblasts reduced C18:0/C18:1 ceramides.
source: As expected, reducing CERS1 expression in human primary myoblasts reduced C18:0 /C18:1 ceramides (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by measurement of ceramide levels in adenovirus-transduced human primary myoblasts (Figure 4A).

claim: CERS1 inhibition increased very long chain C24:0/C24:1 ceramides in human primary myoblasts.
source: Similar to mouse tissue and cells, CERS1 inhibition increased very long chain C24:0 /C24:1 ceramides (Figure 4A) and C24:0 /C24:1 dihydroceramides (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F) and impaired myogenic differentiation, as indicated by immunostaining (Figure 4B) of differentiating myoblasts showing smaller myotube diameter, myotube area and reduction in multinucleated myotubes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G–I) and expression profiling (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by measurement of ceramide levels in adenovirus-transduced human primary myoblasts (Figure 4A).

claim: CERS1 inhibition increased very long chain C24:0/C24:1 dihydroceramides in human primary myoblasts.
source: Similar to mouse tissue and cells, CERS1 inhibition increased very long chain C24:0 /C24:1 ceramides (Figure 4A) and C24:0 /C24:1 dihydroceramides (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F) and impaired myogenic differentiation, as indicated by immunostaining (Figure 4B) of differentiating myoblasts showing smaller myotube diameter, myotube area and reduction in multinucleated myotubes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G–I) and expression profiling (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by measurement of dihydroceramide levels in adenovirus-transduced human primary myoblasts (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).

claim: CERS1 inhibition impaired myogenic differentiation in human primary myoblasts.
source: Similar to mouse tissue and cells, CERS1 inhibition increased very long chain C24:0 /C24:1 ceramides (Figure 4A) and C24:0 /C24:1 dihydroceramides (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F) and impaired myogenic differentiation, as indicated by immunostaining (Figure 4B) of differentiating myoblasts showing smaller myotube diameter, myotube area and reduction in multinucleated myotubes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G–I) and expression profiling (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining, quantification of myotube parameters, and gene expression profiling in CERS1-deficient human primary myoblasts (Figure 4B, Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1G–I).

claim: Exposure of C. elegans to P053 reduced muscle function at the onset of worm aging (day 5).
source: Exposure of C. elegans to P053 mixed within the agar (50 µM and 100 µM) reduced muscle function at the onset of worm aging (day 5) when movement distance and speed are declining (Figure 4D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by measurement of traveled distance and speed in P053-treated C. elegans (Figure 4D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–B).

claim: P053 treatment deteriorated muscle morphology in C. elegans at day 5.
source: In line with our observation of reduced muscle function when using P053 in mice, imaging muscle fibers of P053-treated worms showed deteriorated muscle morphology at day 5 as shown by the presence of rigged fibers compared to the smoother muscle fibers observed in the control worms that were exposed to DMSO vehicle (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging of muscle fibers in P053-treated C. elegans (Figure 4E).

claim: Feeding RW1596 worms with RNAi targeting the lagr-1 transcript reduced its expression by approximately 80%.
source: Feeding RW1596 worms with an interference RNA (RNAi) targeting the lagr-1 transcript reduced its expression by ≈80% (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), and reduced worm muscle function as measured by traveled distance and movement speed (Figure 4F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by measurement of lagr-1 gene expression in RNAi-treated C. elegans (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).

claim: lagr-1 RNAi reduced worm muscle function as measured by traveled distance and movement speed.
source: Feeding RW1596 worms with an interference RNA (RNAi) targeting the lagr-1 transcript reduced its expression by ≈80% (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), and reduced worm muscle function as measured by traveled distance and movement speed (Figure 4F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by measurement of traveled distance and speed in lagr-1 RNAi-treated C. elegans (Figure 4F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).

claim: lagr-1 RNAi treatment deteriorated muscle fibers in worms at day 5.
source: Assessment of muscle fiber morphology revealed deteriorated muscle fibers in worms treated with lagr-1 RNAi at day 5 (Figure 4G).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging of muscle fibers in lagr-1 RNAi-treated C. elegans (Figure 4G).

claim: Inhibition of Cers1 using P053 reduced worm lifespan.
source: Moreover, inhibition of Cers1 using P053 reduced worm lifespan (Figure 4H)
evidence: Supported by lifespan measurement in P053-treated C. elegans (Figure 4H).

claim: Three independent common genetic variants significantly alter CERS1 expression in human skeletal muscle.
source: By exploring the Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) dataset, we discovered three independent (linkage disequilibrium r2 <0.1; Figure 5—figure supplement 1E), common genetic variants that significantly alter CERS1 expression in human skeletal muscle (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by analysis of the GTEx dataset showing three independent eQTLs for CERS1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).

claim: The C-allele at rs117558072 reduces muscle CERS1 expression.
source: The C-allele at rs117558072 and the G-allele at rs1122821 reduce muscle CERS1 expression, while the T-allele at rs71332140 increases muscle CERS1 expression.
evidence: Supported by analysis of the GTEx dataset showing allelic effects on CERS1 expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).

claim: The G-allele at rs1122821 reduces muscle CERS1 expression.
source: The C-allele at rs117558072 and the G-allele at rs1122821 reduce muscle CERS1 expression, while the T-allele at rs71332140 increases muscle CERS1 expression.
evidence: Supported by analysis of the GTEx dataset showing allelic effects on CERS1 expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).

claim: The T-allele at rs71332140 increases muscle CERS1 expression.
source: The C-allele at rs117558072 and the G-allele at rs1122821 reduce muscle CERS1 expression, while the T-allele at rs71332140 increases muscle CERS1 expression.
evidence: Supported by analysis of the GTEx dataset showing allelic effects on CERS1 expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).

claim: A decrease in muscular CERS1 expression leads to impaired overall health rating in humans.
source: Combined results of the Mendelian randomization analysis showed that a decrease in muscular CERS1 expression leads to impaired overall health rating and grip strength (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by Mendelian randomization analysis in the UK biobank (Figure 5A).

claim: A decrease in muscular CERS1 expression leads to reduced grip strength in humans.
source: Combined results of the Mendelian randomization analysis showed that a decrease in muscular CERS1 expression leads to impaired overall health rating and grip strength (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by Mendelian randomization analysis in the UK biobank (Figure 5A).

claim: There is a linear relationship between the eQTL-mediated effect sizes on muscle CERS1 expression and the eQTL-mediated effect sizes on overall health, right grip strength, and left grip strength.
source: Notably, we find a linear relationship between the eQTL-mediated effect sizes on muscle CERS1 expression and the eQTL-mediated effect sizes on the respective phenotypes (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by scatter plot showing linear relationship in Mendelian randomization analysis (Figure 5B).

claim: The large majority of the significant rare variants in the CERS1 coding region (9 out of 11) showed negative effect sizes on overall health rating, right grip strength and left grip strength.
source: Assessing the association of such coding variants with overall health rating, right grip strength and left grip strength, we found that the large majority of the significant (suggestive significant association, p<0.05) variants in the CERS1 coding region (9 out of 11) showed negative effect sizes on overall health rating, right grip strength and left grip strength (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by association analysis of rare coding variants in the UK biobank (Figure 5C).

claim: Inhibition of Cers1 together with Cers2 alleviated the impaired differentiation of C2C12 myoblasts that is observed with Cers1 knockdown alone.
source: Results showed that inhibition of Cers1 together with Cers2 alleviated the impaired differentiation of C2C12 myoblasts that is observed with Cers1 knockdown alone (Figure 5D–E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1G–I).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and gene expression profiling in C2C12 cells with double knockdown of Cers1 and Cers2 (Figure 5D–E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1G–I).

claim: Very long chain ceramides might drive at least some of the negative muscular consequences observed upon reduced Cers1 function.
source: These findings suggest that very long chain ceramides might drive at least some of the negative muscular consequences observed upon reduced Cers1 function.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that double knockdown of Cers1 and Cers2 alleviates impaired differentiation seen with Cers1 knockdown alone.

claim: Three to 8% muscle mass and strength are lost yearly after 30 years of age during normal human aging.
source: Three to 8% muscle mass and strength are lost yearly after 30 years of age and 6–15% after 65 years of age during normal human aging (Melton, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Melton, 2000).

claim: 6–15% muscle mass and strength are lost yearly after 65 years of age during normal human aging.
source: Three to 8% muscle mass and strength are lost yearly after 30 years of age and 6–15% after 65 years of age during normal human aging (Melton, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Melton, 2000).

claim: Sarcopenia predicts and correlates with mortality.
source: Exacerbated age-related loss of muscle mass and strength has recently been recognized as the disease sarcopenia, which predicts and correlates with mortality (Cruz-Jentoft et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Cruz-Jentoft et al., 2010).

claim: The prevalence of sarcopenia in the common 60+year-old population is 10–20%.
source: The importance of sarcopenia is further highlighted by the high prevalence of sarcopenia in the common 60+year-old population (10–20%; Shafiee et al., 2017), especially considering that sarcopenia is one of the leading causes for frailty, loss of independence and reduced quality of life (Rizzoli et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Shafiee et al., 2017).

claim: Sarcopenia is one of the leading causes for frailty, loss of independence and reduced quality of life.
source: The importance of sarcopenia is further highlighted by the high prevalence of sarcopenia in the common 60+year-old population (10–20%; Shafiee et al., 2017), especially considering that sarcopenia is one of the leading causes for frailty, loss of independence and reduced quality of life (Rizzoli et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Rizzoli et al., 2013).

claim: Recent evidence suggests the involvement of sphingolipids in skeletal muscle homeostasis upon aging.
source: Recent evidence further suggests the involvement of sphingolipids in skeletal muscle homeostasis upon aging (Tan-Chen et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Tan-Chen et al., 2020).

claim: Sphingolipids have been shown to be involved in skeletal muscle bioenergetics.
source: While sphingolipids have been shown to be involved in skeletal muscle bioenergetics (Turner et al., 2018; Park et al., 2016), insulin sensitivity (Holland et al., 2007) and diabetes (Zhao et al., 2007), the contribution of ceramides to skeletal muscle aging is not well understood.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Turner et al., 2018; Park et al., 2016).

claim: Sphingolipids have been shown to be involved in insulin sensitivity.
source: While sphingolipids have been shown to be involved in skeletal muscle bioenergetics (Turner et al., 2018; Park et al., 2016), insulin sensitivity (Holland et al., 2007) and diabetes (Zhao et al., 2007), the contribution of ceramides to skeletal muscle aging is not well understood.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Holland et al., 2007).

claim: Sphingolipids have been shown to be involved in diabetes.
source: While sphingolipids have been shown to be involved in skeletal muscle bioenergetics (Turner et al., 2018; Park et al., 2016), insulin sensitivity (Holland et al., 2007) and diabetes (Zhao et al., 2007), the contribution of ceramides to skeletal muscle aging is not well understood.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Zhao et al., 2007).

claim: The first enzyme of the de novo sphingolipid biosynthesis pathway (SPT) is involved in skeletal muscle aging.
source: We recently reported that the first enzyme of the de novo sphingolipid biosynthesis pathway (SPT) is involved in skeletal muscle aging (Laurila et al., 2022b).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Laurila et al., 2022b).

claim: Six ceramide synthases (Cers1-6) catalyze ceramide synthesis in mammals resulting in a range of ceramides from C14:0 to C36:0.
source: Six ceramide synthases (Cers1-6) catalyze ceramide synthesis in mammals resulting in a range of ceramides from C14:0 to C36:0 (Turner et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Turner et al., 2018).

claim: Cers1 only uses 18 carbon (C18) fatty acids to create C18 (d18:1/18:0) ceramides.
source: For example, Cers1 only uses 18 carbon (C18) fatty acids to create C18 (d18:1/18:0) ceramides, whereas Cers2 predominantly synthesizes d18:1/24:0 (C24:0) and d18:1/24:1 (C24:1) ceramides and Cers5 uses C16 acyl‐CoA substrates for acylation of the free primary amine group of sphingoid bases to form the corresponding C16:0 ceramides (Mizutani et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Mizutani et al., 2005).

claim: Cers2 predominantly synthesizes d18:1/24:0 (C24:0) and d18:1/24:1 (C24:1) ceramides.
source: For example, Cers1 only uses 18 carbon (C18) fatty acids to create C18 (d18:1/18:0) ceramides, whereas Cers2 predominantly synthesizes d18:1/24:0 (C24:0) and d18:1/24:1 (C24:1) ceramides and Cers5 uses C16 acyl‐CoA substrates for acylation of the free primary amine group of sphingoid bases to form the corresponding C16:0 ceramides (Mizutani et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Mizutani et al., 2005).

claim: Cers5 uses C16 acyl‐CoA substrates for acylation of the free primary amine group of sphingoid bases to form the corresponding C16:0 ceramides.
source: For example, Cers1 only uses 18 carbon (C18) fatty acids to create C18 (d18:1/18:0) ceramides, whereas Cers2 predominantly synthesizes d18:1/24:0 (C24:0) and d18:1/24:1 (C24:1) ceramides and Cers5 uses C16 acyl‐CoA substrates for acylation of the free primary amine group of sphingoid bases to form the corresponding C16:0 ceramides (Mizutani et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Mizutani et al., 2005).

claim: Cers1 and Cers5 are the two most expressed ceramide synthases in skeletal muscle.
source: Cers1 and Cers5 are the two most expressed ceramide synthases in skeletal muscle (Levy and Futerman, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Levy and Futerman, 2010).

claim: Reducing Cers1 function by genetic or pharmacological means has been shown to reduce adiposity and body weight upon exposing mice to a high fat diet.
source: Reducing Cers1 function by genetic or pharmacological means has been shown to reduce adiposity and body weight upon exposing mice to a high fat diet (Turner et al., 2018; Gosejacob et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Turner et al., 2018; Gosejacob et al., 2016).

claim: BMI was found to correlate with C18:0 ceramide species.
source: Moreover, BMI was found to correlate with C18:0 ceramide species, pointing towards Cers1 as a desirable target for metabolic interventions (Weir et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Weir et al., 2013).

claim: Skeletal muscle-specific deletion of Cers1 in young mice reduces muscle fiber size and force.
source: On the other hand, recent evidence demonstrates that skeletal muscle-specific deletion of Cers1 in young mice reduces muscle fiber size and force, suggesting that Cers1 is needed for proper skeletal muscle function in young mice (Tosetti et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Tosetti et al., 2020).

claim: CERS1 has been shown to synthesize C18:0 and C18:1 ceramides.
source: CERS1 has been shown to synthesize C18:0 and C18:1 ceramides (Mizutani et al., 2005; Ginkel et al., 2012; Venkataraman et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Mizutani et al., 2005; Ginkel et al., 2012; Venkataraman et al., 2002).

claim: Ceramide levels, and particularly Cers1-derived C18-ceramides were previously found elevated in skeletal muscle upon high-fat diet.
source: Ceramide levels, and particularly Cers1-derived C18-ceramides were previously found elevated in skeletal muscle upon high-fat diet (Lanza et al., 2013), streptozotocin-induced diabetes (Zabielski et al., 2014) and in obese, diabetic patients (Bergman et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Lanza et al., 2013).

claim: Cers1-derived C18-ceramides were previously found elevated in skeletal muscle in streptozotocin-induced diabetes.
source: Ceramide levels, and particularly Cers1-derived C18-ceramides were previously found elevated in skeletal muscle upon high-fat diet (Lanza et al., 2013), streptozotocin-induced diabetes (Zabielski et al., 2014) and in obese, diabetic patients (Bergman et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Zabielski et al., 2014).

claim: Cers1-derived C18-ceramides were previously found elevated in skeletal muscle in obese, diabetic patients.
source: Ceramide levels, and particularly Cers1-derived C18-ceramides were previously found elevated in skeletal muscle upon high-fat diet (Lanza et al., 2013), streptozotocin-induced diabetes (Zabielski et al., 2014) and in obese, diabetic patients (Bergman et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Bergman et al., 2016).

claim: The isoform-specific Cers1 inhibitor P053 reduced C18 ceramide species (while increasing C24 ceramides) exclusively in skeletal muscle, which reduced fat mass in mice fed a high-fat diet.
source: Indeed, the isoform-specific Cers1 inhibitor P053 reduced C18 ceramide species (while increasing C24 ceramides) exclusively in skeletal muscle, which reduced fat mass in mice fed a high-fat diet (Turner et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Turner et al., 2018).

claim: Cers1 deficiency from birth was previously reported to cause defects in foliation, progressive shrinkage, and neuronal apoptosis in the cerebellum.
source: Furthermore, intact Cers1 might not only be important for skeletal muscle homeostasis in aging; Cers1 deficiency from birth was previously also reported to cause defects in foliation, progressive shrinkage, and neuronal apoptosis in the cerebellum, which translated to functional deficits including impaired exploration of novel objects, locomotion, and motor coordination (Ginkel et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Ginkel et al., 2012).

claim: Compensation effects in brain and liver have been reported in Cers2 knockout mice.
source: Of note, compensation effects in brain and liver have also been reported in Cers2 knockout mice (Pewzner-Jung et al., 2010; Imgrund et al., 2009), and upregulation of Cers2 to compensate for Cers1 deficiency in neurons reduced long chain C24:0 /C24:1 ceramides and hence, ameliorated Cers1 deficiency-mediated neurodegeneration (Spassieva et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Pewzner-Jung et al., 2010; Imgrund et al., 2009).

claim: Upregulation of Cers2 to compensate for Cers1 deficiency in neurons reduced long chain C24:0/C24:1 ceramides and ameliorated Cers1 deficiency-mediated neurodegeneration.
source: Of note, compensation effects in brain and liver have also been reported in Cers2 knockout mice (Pewzner-Jung et al., 2010; Imgrund et al., 2009), and upregulation of Cers2 to compensate for Cers1 deficiency in neurons reduced long chain C24:0 /C24:1 ceramides and hence, ameliorated Cers1 deficiency-mediated neurodegeneration (Spassieva et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Spassieva et al., 2016).

claim: Sptlc1 inactivation has highly beneficial effects on healthy aging.
source: Given the highly beneficial effects of Sptlc1 inactivation on healthy aging (Laurila et al., 2022b), our current study further suggests that a significant part of the benefits of blocking the de novo ceramide biosynthesis pathway might come from inhibiting very long chain ceramides.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Laurila et al., 2022b).

claim: The compensatory upregulation of CERS2 derived very long chain ceramide and dihydroceramide species in aging might accelerate age-related muscle wasting and dysfunction.
source: Due to our consistent observation of increased very long chain C24:0 /C24:1 ceramides and dihydroceramides upon Cers1/CERS1 inhibition, we suggest a molecular network in which the compensatory upregulation of CERS2 derived very long chain ceramide and dihydroceramide species in aging might accelerate age-related muscle wasting and dysfunction, hence contributing to sarcopenia (Figure 5F).
evidence: Inferred from the consistent observation of increased C24:0/C24:1 ceramides and dihydroceramides upon Cers1 inhibition and the alleviation of impaired differentiation when both Cers1 and Cers2 are knocked down.

claim: The 65+year-old population is prospected to double by the year 2050.
source: We are currently experiencing the biggest demographic shift in human history with a prospective doubling of the 65+year-old population by the year 2050, thereby constituting almost a quarter of the world's population for the first time (Bloom et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Bloom et al., 2015).

claim: One-fifth of an individual's life will be lived with morbidity and reduced mobility.
source: While the increase in human lifespan could provide unprecedented opportunities for aged individuals, healthspan is not quite following this trend: One-fifth of an individual's life will be lived with morbidity and reduced mobility (Partridge et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Partridge et al., 2018).

claim: There has been a 20% increase in healthcare spending due to the growing elderly population in the last 10 years.
source: Health burden escalates with age, which not only incapacitates the elderly but also puts tremendous stress on the healthcare system exemplified by the 20% increased healthcare spending due to the growing elderly population in the last 10 years alone (Atella et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Atella et al., 2019).
